title: Dependency Injection Patterns
description: Master advanced DI patterns, service lifetimes, decorator pattern, and build testable, maintainable architectures.

data.text: Dependency Injection (DI) is a design pattern that implements Inversion of Control (IoC). It decouples components by injecting dependencies rather than having components create them directly. This improves testability, maintainability, and flexibility.

data.title: Avoid Service Locator
data.text: Service Locator is an anti-pattern. It hides dependencies and makes code harder to test. Prefer constructor injection for required dependencies.

.NET's built-in DI container supports three service lifetimes: Transient (new instance each time), Scoped (one instance per scope), and Singleton (one instance for app lifetime). Choosing the right lifetime is critical for correctness and performance.

data.title: Service Lifetime Configuration
Capturing Scoped Services in Singletons
data.text: Never inject a scoped service into a singleton. This causes the scoped service to become effectively singleton, leading to incorrect behavior and potential thread safety issues. Use IServiceProvider or factory pattern instead.

data.title: Correct Pattern: Singleton Using Scoped Service

data.text: The decorator pattern allows you to add behavior to services without modifying them. This is useful for caching, logging, retry logic, authentication, and other cross-cutting concerns.

data.title: Decorator Pattern Implementation
Scrutor for Easy Decoration
data.text: The Scrutor library provides fluent syntax for decorator registration. Use .Decorate<>() instead of manual registration for cleaner code.
When you need to create instances with runtime parameters, use the factory pattern. .NET provides built-in support for factory-based service creation.

data.title: Factory Pattern

data.text: DI makes testing easy by allowing you to inject mock implementations. Use mocking frameworks like Moq, NSubstitute, or FakeItEasy to create test doubles.

data.title: Advanced DI Registration
Key Takeaways
points: Use constructor injection for required dependencies, avoid service locator
Choose service lifetimes carefully: Transient for stateless, Scoped for per-request, Singleton for app-wide
Never inject scoped services into singletons - create scopes when needed
Decorator pattern enables clean cross-cutting concerns (caching, logging, retry)
Factory pattern handles runtime parameter creation
DI enables easy testing with mock implementations
Use keyed services (.NET 8+) for multiple implementations of the same interface
TryAdd pattern allows clean override of default registrations
data.takeaway: Dependency Injection is fundamental to modern .NET architecture. Understanding service lifetimes, avoiding common anti-patterns, and using advanced patterns like decorators and factories will help you build maintainable, testable applications.
